mastery.question_text:
A quadrilateral has $AB \perp BC$ and $BC \perp CD$.
What relationship must $AB$ and $CD$ have?
mastery.solution_text:
Both $AB$ and $CD$ are perpendicular to $BC$.
They run in the same direction, so $AB$ and $CD$ are parallel, not perpendicular.

mastery.question_text:
In the figure, $PQ \perp RS$.
Is $\angle POT$ necessarily $90^{\circ}$?
Explain.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large},scale=0.9]
\draw (-2,0) node[left] {$P$}--(2,0) node[right] {$Q$}; \draw (0,-2) node[below] {$R$}--(0,2) node[above] {$S$}; \draw (0,0) node[below left] {$O$}--(55:1.8) node[above right] {$T$};
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
mastery.solution_text: No. The perpendicular statement fixes the angles between $PQ$ and $RS$ only. Since $OT$ is a different ray, $\angle POT$ is not guaranteed to be $90^{\circ}$.

mastery.question_text:
A map shows one street running north-south and another east-west, but their drawn segments stop short of each other.
Are the streets' full lines perpendicular?
mastery.solution_text:
North-south and east-west directions meet at $90^{\circ}$ when extended.
Yes, the full street lines are perpendicular.
